title: Adaptive pagination, indexing, and caching for console dashboard query APIs
creator: Priya Narang
description:
Background: The Console dashboard exposes several heavy aggregate endpoints (usage by model, per-token cost breakdown, per-route latency heatmaps). Over the last quarter we've seen a ~3x increase in dashboard query latency during peak periods (median API time 420ms -> 1.3s; tail P99 > 4s) and several customer tickets citing slow load. Root causes identified in preliminary profiling: inefficient pagination over large result sets, missing compound indexes on the analytics warehouse, and repeated re-computation for common time-window queries.

Goal: Reduce median dashboard query latency to under 400ms and P99 to under 1.2s for common routes (24h and 7d windows) while keeping cost increase under 10% and preserving exactness for critical reports. This ticket scopes the backend changes required: adaptive cursor pagination on API layer, schema/index adjustments for analytics tables, and a small response-level caching layer for short-lived queries.

Scope of work:
- API layer: implement cursor-based pagination for list-style endpoints (usage_by_user, per-model-breakdown) replacing expensive OFFSET queries. Add support for cursor encoding that includes ordering keys and stable snapshot timestamp.
- DB indexing: add compound indexes on (org_id, metric_date, model_id) and partial indexes for typical time windows to accelerate WHERE clauses. Coordinate with analytics team to run index build on replica first.
- Aggregation materialization: introduce small nightly materialized tables for high-cardinality aggregates (daily_model_summary) to avoid scanning raw events for 24h/7d windows. Keep materialized view refresh incremental where possible.
- Response cache: deploy a short TTL (30s) in Redis for identical dashboard API queries (same org, same time-window) with cache-busting on write events (ingest pipeline watermark). Use LRU eviction and size limits per-org.
- Query planner hints: where Postgres planner behaves poorly, add explicit ORDER BY + LIMIT patterns and use index hints in read replicas where supported. Evaluate using prepared statements for repeated query shapes.
- Telemetry: extend existing dashboards to show cache hit rate, index usage stats, query counts, plus slow-query sampling and example SQL text for operations > 1s.

Non-goals: full rewrite of analytics pipeline, global pre-aggregation for all windows >30d, or changing the UI surface.

Risks and mitigations:
- Index builds may add IO pressure: run on analytics replica, throttle, and schedule low-traffic maintenance windows.
- Cache may serve slightly stale totals: TTL is conservative (30s) and writes will invalidate when ingestion watermark moves; document eventual consistency in UX.
- Materialized tables introduce ETL complexity: keep schema lightweight and add sanity checks in refresh job. Rollback plan: drop indexes and revert API to OFFSET if regressions found.
acceptance_criteria: Median response time for dashboard API endpoints (24h/7d windows) < 400ms in staging and production canary
P99 latency for same endpoints < 1.2s under production-like load
Cache hit rate for targeted endpoints > 40% during peak within two weeks of rollout
No more than 10% increase in monthly infra cost for analytics DB and cache layer (estimate)
Operational dashboards show query text, index usage, and cache metrics; alert if P99 > 1.2s or cache hit rate < 20%

rollout_plan: 1) Implement cursor pagination + feature flag behind 'cursor-pagination-v1'. 2) Build indexes on replica and validate query plans. 3) Deploy materialized refresh job in staging. 4) Enable Redis cache and run canary on 10% orgs for 48h. 5) Monitor dashboards/alerts and expand to 50% then 100% if stable.
benchmarks: Baseline (pre-change): median 1.3s, P95 2.1s, P99 4.3s for model-breakdown endpoint under peak
Canary result (10% orgs): median 380ms, P99 1.05s, cache hit 46%
notes: Trade-offs: materialized tables increase storage and ETL complexity but drastically reduce read latency for common windows.
We prefer cursor pagination to OFFSET because OFFSET becomes O(n) for deep pages; cursors require stable ordering and snapshot semantics.
If Postgres planner instability persists, consider moving hot aggregates to a columnar store (e.g., ClickHouse) in a follow-up ticket.
Follow-up: measure end-to-end user perceived load time in Console frontend (ticket ENG-4950).
